scenes.headline: Why a hidden state gives the prompt back
scenes.sub: Transformers are almost surely injective, and SipIt inverts them exactly.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Moss! Every part of a transformer loses information. So the hidden state must be a lossy summary of your prompt. It isn't.

scenes.label: Lossy parts, injective whole
scenes.text: Two different prompts almost surely never reach the same hidden state. So a hidden state is the prompt in another basis, and it can be read back.

scenes.title: Why a collision has probability zero

items.say: Softmax, LayerNorm and smooth activations are real-analytic, and so is the whole network, as a function of its weights.

items.text: Collisions sit on a thin slice
items.say: So for two prompts, the weights where they collide form a thin slice with no volume.
A random initializer lands there with probability zero.
And gradient steps can't squash volume onto it.

scenes.label: prompt pairs searched per model, with zero collisions
scenes.note: exhaustive on GPT-2 Small and Gemma3-1B; larger models were sampled
scenes.say: The authors went hunting for collisions: over three hundred forty-three billion prompt pairs per model. They found none.

scenes.title: SipIt: rebuild the prompt token by token

steps.say: SipIt starts from the hidden states at every position, say a leaked KV-cache.
The model is causal, so each position depends on the prefix and one new token. Try a candidate.
If its state matches the observed one, within a tolerance, that's the token. Almost surely, only one does.
Append it and move on. The work is linear in the prompt's length.
Gradients pick the order, so it explores under a quarter of one percent of the vocabulary.

scenes.title: Seconds to recover a prompt, GPT-2 Small
scenes.note: SipIt and brute force: 100% exact. HardPrompts: 0%
scenes.say: Brute force recovers every prompt too, slowly. SipIt takes about twenty-eight seconds, and is just as exact.

scenes.text: A hidden state is not a summary of the prompt. It is the prompt, in another basis.
